_about: Build standards, layer "every product" (#136, spec #127). Applies to every product a run builds. Format and checker: .claude/harness/lib/standards.js, bin/check-standards.js. ASVS refs are OWASP ASVS 5.0.0 requirement ids; WCAG refs are WCAG 2.2 success criteria. A topic with no source is listed under gaps, never invented.

layer.title: Every product
layer.appliesWhen: Always: every product built by a run gets this layer.

standards.title: No secrets in the code
standards.mustBeTrue: API keys, passwords and tokens come from environment variables or a secret manager; none is in source files or in git history.

test.how: A secret scan of tracked files and of the branch history finds nothing (for example .claude/harness/bin/scan-secrets.js in CI).

standards.why: A secret in the repository is readable by everyone who can read the code, forever, even after it is deleted.

standards.title: Every input is checked on the server
standards.mustBeTrue: Every request field is validated on the server against an allow list or an expected structure (type, length, range, format) before it is used.

test.how: For each endpoint, a request with a wrong type, an over-long value and an out-of-range value is rejected with a 4xx response and nothing is stored.

standards.why: Browser checks can be skipped by anyone; unchecked input is how most injection and data-corruption bugs start.

standards.title: Database queries cannot be injected
standards.mustBeTrue: Database queries use parameters, an ORM or a query builder; user input is never joined into a query string.

test.how: A search or lookup with an injection payload (for example a quote and OR 1=1) returns no extra rows and no error; a lint or grep finds no query built by string concatenation.

standards.why: SQL injection lets an attacker read or change any data in the database.

standards.title: User content is shown as text, never run
standards.mustBeTrue: Content that came from users is encoded for the place it is shown (HTML, attribute, URL, script), and user-supplied HTML is sanitized.

test.how: A journey saves content containing a script tag and an event-handler attribute; the page shows it as text and no script runs.

standards.why: Cross-site scripting runs an attacker's code in another user's browser, with that user's session.

standards.title: Pages send a Content Security Policy
standards.mustBeTrue: Every HTML response carries a Content-Security-Policy header that limits where scripts and objects load from (at least object-src 'none' and base-uri 'none') and sets frame-ancestors.

test.how: A test fetches each page type and asserts the header and its directives.

standards.why: A policy stops most injected scripts from running even when an encoding mistake slips through, and stops the page being framed for clickjacking.

standards.title: HTTPS only, with HSTS
standards.mustBeTrue: All traffic between users and the product uses TLS with a publicly trusted certificate, with no fallback to plain HTTP; responses carry Strict-Transport-Security with a max-age of at least one year.

test.how: A test against the deployed staging site: plain HTTP redirects to HTTPS, and the HSTS header is present with max-age >= 31536000.

standards.why: Without TLS anyone on the network path can read or change passwords, sessions and data.

standards.title: Browsers may not guess content types
standards.mustBeTrue: Every response carries X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and a Content-Type that matches its body, with a charset.

test.how: A test fetches a page, a JSON response and a static file and asserts both headers.

standards.why: Content-type guessing lets an uploaded or returned file be run as a script.

standards.title: Other sites cannot act for a signed-in user
standards.mustBeTrue: Every state-changing request uses POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE and is protected against cross-site request forgery (a token, a checked Origin header, or SameSite cookies plus a preflight-forcing content type).

test.how: A state-changing request sent with a foreign Origin, or without the CSRF token, is rejected and changes nothing; a GET to the same route changes nothing.

standards.why: Without it, any web page the user visits can submit actions in their name.

standards.title: Cross-origin access only for listed sites
standards.mustBeTrue: Access-Control-Allow-Origin is a fixed value or checked against an allow list; a wildcard is only used for public data with no credentials.

test.how: A request with an unlisted Origin gets no Access-Control-Allow-Origin for it; a listed one does.

standards.why: An open CORS policy lets any site read a signed-in user's data through their browser.

standards.title: Users can reach only what they are allowed to
standards.mustBeTrue: Every function and every data item is checked against the caller's permissions on the server; nothing relies on hidden buttons or client-side checks.

test.how: For each resource type, user A requesting user B's item by id gets 403 or 404 and no data; a non-admin calling an admin route is refused.

standards.why: Broken access control (reading another user's data by changing an id) is the most common serious web flaw.

standards.title: No secrets in web addresses
standards.mustBeTrue: Session tokens, API keys and other sensitive values travel in headers or the request body, never in the URL or query string.

test.how: A test walks the API routes and asserts that no route takes a token or key as a query parameter; logs of a journey contain no token in a URL.

standards.why: URLs end up in browser history, server logs and the Referer header sent to other sites.

standards.title: Nothing for developers is left on the live site
standards.mustBeTrue: In production, debug modes are off, the .git folder and other source-control metadata are not served, and test code, sample pages and developer tools are not deployed.

test.how: A test against staging asserts that /.git/HEAD and a debug route return 404 and that error pages show no debug output.

standards.why: Debug output and source metadata hand attackers the code and the configuration.

standards.title: Errors tell users little, logs tell developers enough
standards.mustBeTrue: An unexpected error returns a generic message to the user (no stack trace, query, file path, secret or token); the detail goes to the server log.

test.how: A forced server error returns a generic body with no stack trace or internal path, and the same error appears in the log with its detail.

standards.why: Error details tell an attacker which software, queries and files to target.

standards.title: A failure never lets an action through
standards.mustBeTrue: When validation or a dependency fails, the action is refused; nothing is processed on the error path (fail closed).

test.how: A test makes the validator or a downstream call throw and asserts that the action was not performed and no partial record was saved.

standards.why: Fail-open bugs process payments or grant access precisely when something has gone wrong.

standards.title: One handler catches anything unexpected
standards.mustBeTrue: A last-resort handler catches every unhandled error, logs it and returns a generic response, so the process keeps serving other users.

test.how: A route that throws an unexpected error returns a generic 500, the error is logged, and the next request succeeds.

standards.why: An uncaught error can take the whole product down or lose the error detail needed to fix it.

standards.title: Passwords and tokens never reach the logs
standards.mustBeTrue: Logs never contain passwords, secrets, full session tokens or payment details; values that must be traced are masked or hashed.

test.how: A test logs a request containing a password, a token and an API key and asserts that none appears in the log output.

standards.why: Logs are copied widely and kept long; a secret in a log is a leaked secret.

standards.title: Each log line says when, where, who and what
standards.mustBeTrue: Each log entry has a UTC (or offset) timestamp, the component, the acting user or client, and the event, in a format the log tool can parse.

test.how: A test captures a log entry for a request and asserts the timestamp format, component, user id and event fields.

standards.why: Without these fields an incident cannot be reconstructed.

standards.title: User input cannot forge log lines
standards.mustBeTrue: Values written to logs are encoded so user input cannot add lines or break the log format.

test.how: A test logs a value containing a newline and a fake log prefix and asserts the output is one entry with the value escaped.

standards.why: Forged log lines hide an attack or frame another user.

standards.title: Refused access and bypass attempts are logged
standards.mustBeTrue: Failed authorization attempts and attempts to bypass validation or rate limits are logged as security events.

test.how: A refused request (another user's item, a rate-limited call, an invalid payload) produces a security log entry naming the user and the rule.

standards.why: These events are the early warning of an attack in progress.

standards.title: No libraries with known holes
standards.mustBeTrue: Dependencies have no known vulnerabilities above the severity the project allows, checked on every pull request.

test.how: CI runs the package manager's audit (for example npm audit --audit-level=high) and fails on a finding.

standards.why: Most breaches of small products come through an outdated library, not the product's own code.

standards.title: Exact library versions are pinned
standards.mustBeTrue: The lock file is committed and CI installs from it (for example npm ci), so every build uses the same versions.

test.how: CI fails if the lock file is missing or out of date with the manifest.

standards.why: Unpinned installs can pull a different, compromised version between test and release.

standards.title: Everything works with a keyboard
standards.mustBeTrue: Every action can be done with a keyboard alone, and focus never gets stuck; dialogs keep focus inside while open and give it back on close.

test.how: A keyboard-only journey (Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, Escape) completes each key task, opens and closes each dialog, and focus returns to the trigger.

standards.why: People who cannot use a mouse, and screen-reader users, depend on the keyboard.

standards.title: You can always see where you are
standards.mustBeTrue: The keyboard focus is always visible and is not hidden behind sticky headers, banners or other content.

test.how: The keyboard journey takes a screenshot at each focus stop and asserts a visible focus indicator inside the viewport; an automated accessibility scan reports no focus issue.

standards.why: Without a visible focus a keyboard user is lost on the page.

standards.title: Buttons are big enough to hit
standards.mustBeTrue: Interactive targets are at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels (44 by 44 points on native apps), or have that much space around them.

test.how: A browser test measures every button and link on the key screens and fails on one below 24x24 without the spacing exception.

standards.why: Small targets are hard to hit for people with limited dexterity and on phones.

standards.title: Every image and control has a name
standards.mustBeTrue: Images that carry meaning have text alternatives, and every control (including icon-only buttons) has an accessible name, role and state.

test.how: An automated accessibility scan (for example axe) on every key screen reports no missing names or alternatives.

standards.why: Screen readers announce unnamed controls as "button" or skip them.

standards.title: Text and controls are readable
standards.mustBeTrue: Text has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text), and controls and their states at least 3:1 against what is next to them.

test.how: The accessibility scan on each key screen, in light and dark themes, reports no contrast failure.

standards.why: Low contrast makes the product unreadable for people with low vision and in sunlight.

standards.title: Works at 320 pixels wide and when zoomed
standards.mustBeTrue: Content reflows at a width of 320 CSS pixels (400% zoom) without horizontal scrolling or lost content.

test.how: A browser test renders each key screen at 320px wide and asserts no horizontal scroll and that each main control is visible.

standards.why: People who zoom in, and phone users, must not lose content.

standards.title: Form errors say what is wrong and how to fix it
standards.mustBeTrue: A form error names the field in text and, where known, suggests the fix; information already given is not asked for again in the same process.

test.how: A journey submits each form with a wrong value and asserts a text error tied to the field and a suggestion; a multi-step form keeps earlier answers.

standards.why: Colour-only or vague errors block people from finishing a task.

standards.title: At least 80% of the code is run by tests
standards.mustBeTrue: Line coverage of the product's own code is at least 80%, measured by the verify gate, with acceptance tests written by a human and never weakened to pass.

test.how: The verify gate reports coverage and fails below the floor in verify.config.json.

standards.why: Untested code is where regressions hide; the floor is this repository's working agreement.

standards.title: Tests run before every merge
standards.mustBeTrue: Fast checks run on every pull request, and the full gate runs before a pull request is merged.

test.how: The CI workflow runs the fast checks on pull_request events and the full gate on ready pull requests; a failing check blocks the merge.

standards.why: A check that does not run before a merge does not protect the product.
